paragraphs: AffIn-Space addresses a weakness in multimodal language models: their understanding of spatial structure can deteriorate when the viewpoint or viewing distance changes. The authors attribute this fragility to representations that remain tied to the image’s pixel arrangement. That makes it difficult to separate the underlying three-dimensional scene from the camera pose used to observe it.

The framework explicitly separates these factors in two stages. First, it derives affine quantities from pose features and uses them to resample three-dimensional features into a canonical arrangement before combining representations. Second, it applies orthogonal projection inside the language model to remove pose-dependent components from hidden states. Conditional reconstruction helps preserve geometric information that should remain recoverable after this removal.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art results across spatial reasoning and grounding benchmarks, alongside stronger stability under affine perturbations. The significance is that geometric invariance becomes an explicit part of representation construction and internal processing. The reported robustness concerns the tested affine changes, supporting this approach to spatial understanding.
icml-2026-affin-space-learning-affine-in.tldr: AffIn-Space explicitly removes camera-pose effects from representations to improve multimodal models’ spatial understanding and stability under affine changes.

paragraphs: DataGuard investigates whether a dataset was used to train a deep learning model without modifying that dataset beforehand. This matters because auditing methods that alter data can introduce performance or security risks. The goal is quantitative evidence of dataset usage, including cases where training used only part of the collection.

The framework compares the dataset being audited with auxiliary datasets that were not used for training. It then analyzes the information differences between these groups. Formal inequalities provide a basis for distinguishing training data, and a multivariate statistical test combines the discrepancies into auditing scores. These components connect an observed difference to a structured statistical assessment of usage.

The authors report detection of both complete and partial dataset use, with no false positives in their experiments and robustness across varied training scenarios. The absence of false positives is an experimental finding rather than an unconditional guarantee. The contribution is a way to obtain auditing evidence from comparative information signals while leaving the original dataset intact.
icml-2026-dataguard-a-non-intrusive-data.tldr: DataGuard audits training-data usage without altering datasets by combining information comparisons with statistical testing.

paragraphs: DiffCrossGait tackles gait recognition across two different representations: two-dimensional silhouettes and three-dimensional point clouds. Their distributions differ, making it difficult to learn identity features that work across both. The paper extends alignment beyond the final feature vectors by also constraining how the two modalities evolve during a latent diffusion process.

Both modalities receive shared Gaussian noise in a common latent space. A three-phase strategy uses different noise intensities to anchor identity, encourage consistent dynamics, and support recovery of structure across modalities. This creates alignment throughout denoising, encouraging the representations to share both their evolution and their compressed internal structure. The intended result is gait information that depends less on the sensing modality.

The diffusion component is used only as a training objective and is separated from the recognition backbone. Recognition therefore does not require repeated denoising at inference time. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on SUSTech1K and FreeGait. These findings support using richer generative alignment during training while retaining an efficient recognition procedure when the model is deployed.
icml-2026-diffcrossgait-trajectory-level.tldr: DiffCrossGait aligns silhouette and point-cloud gait features throughout diffusion training without adding iterative denoising at inference.

paragraphs: BiCoT aims to identify ownership of reasoning language models while preserving their reasoning quality. Existing black-box watermarking approaches can interfere with final answers or depend on fragile triggers. This paper embeds the ownership signal in the internal geometry associated with reasoning traces, tying it to representations involved in producing coherent reasoning.

The method aligns structurally important anchors with a private signature subspace and regularizes ordinary control tokens to preserve their capacity to carry meaning. The design makes watermark removal difficult without disturbing reasoning-relevant features. For verification, Robust Subspace Registration uses top-k token log probabilities and sentinel tokens. These sentinels help calibrate systematic changes in output distributions caused by model modification or representation drift.

The experiments report preserved reasoning fidelity and robust watermark detection across complex reasoning tasks. Detection remains effective under tested fine-tuning, quantization, model perturbations, and adaptive output attacks, including both familiar and out-of-distribution settings. The results support coupling ownership evidence to reasoning representations and calibrating its detection after changes to the model.
icml-2026-echoes-within-the-reasoning-st.tldr: BiCoT embeds ownership signals in reasoning representations and verifies them through token probabilities while preserving reasoning quality in reported tests.

paragraphs: Experience-Augmented Policy Optimization addresses inefficient reuse of experience when training language models with verifiable rewards. Generating fresh reasoning attempts can be expensive. Reusing complete earlier reasoning trajectories introduces another problem: as the model changes, those fixed trajectories can become poorly matched to its current behavior.

EAPO instead uses a previously reinforcement-trained policy as an action-level source of experience. During a new rollout, it selectively introduces that experience at critical decision points. This allows prior knowledge to influence a newly generated trajectory rather than requiring the current model to follow an old one wholesale. An adapted importance-sampling scheme accounts for the altered rollout process to support stable, unbiased learning.

Experiments using Qwen-2.5-math 7b and Qwen-3-8B across five benchmarks show consistent reasoning improvements over state-of-the-art RLVR methods. The central contribution is a more adaptable form of experience reuse: the prior policy supplies guidance where decisions matter, while the training procedure accounts for how that guidance changes the data being collected.
icml-2026-experience-augmented-policy-op.tldr: EAPO reuses a previously trained reasoning policy as selective action-level guidance and corrects for its influence during learning.

paragraphs: Converting a monocular video into stereo requires synthesizing another viewpoint. Moving the viewpoint exposes regions that were hidden in the original image, leaving gaps that need to be filled. Learning to fill these disocclusions usually relies on scarce stereo pairs or synthetic examples whose appearance can differ from real footage.

The paper develops self-supervision from monocular videos using a geometric cycle. Its Geometric Reciprocity Theorem states that, under nearest-neighbor depth-image-based rendering, the target-view disocclusion mask equals the mask of pixels lost when warping back to the source. This relationship makes the relevant disocclusion masks analytically computable from monocular images and connects the training construction to the masks encountered at test time.

That consistency supports learning from abundant monocular videos without requiring paired stereo footage. The authors report substantial improvements over training-free and supervised state-of-the-art methods. The theorem’s stated nearest-neighbor warping formulation is essential to interpreting the result: it establishes the geometric relationship under that formulation, providing the foundation for the self-supervised training approach.
icml-2026-geometric-reciprocity-unlockin.tldr: A geometric reciprocity result enables self-supervised stereo-video training from monocular footage under a specified nearest-neighbor rendering formulation.

paragraphs: Golden Goose expands the supply of tasks for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Such training needs answers that can be checked, which excludes much reasoning-rich internet text from conventional task construction. The method converts that material into multiple-choice exercises by hiding an important reasoning step and asking the model to recover it.

An LLM selects and masks key steps in a source passage, then generates varied, plausible alternatives. This produces a checkable selection task from material that was not originally a verifiable exercise. The authors build GooseReason-0.7M with more than 0.7 million tasks across mathematics, programming, and general science. They report sustained training gains for models whose improvements had saturated on existing RLVR data.

The reported evaluations achieve new state-of-the-art results for 1.5B and 4B-Instruct models across 15 benchmarks. In cybersecurity, tasks generated from raw FineWeb material enable Qwen3-4B-Instruct to outperform a specialized 7B model. These findings support the potential to expand verifiable training through automated task construction from reasoning-rich text.
icml-2026-golden-goose-a-simple-trick-to.tldr: Golden Goose turns reasoning-rich text into checkable multiple-choice tasks that sustain improvements in reinforcement-trained language models.

paragraphs: Diffusion planners can propose trajectories with attractive predicted rewards that do not fit the environment’s local dynamics. Choosing these plans on value alone can make execution brittle. SAGE adds a consistency assessment when ranking candidate plans, so action selection considers whether the proposed transitions agree with a learned model of short-term behavior.

The method learns a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture encoder from offline state sequences and trains an action-conditioned predictor in the resulting latent space. At test time, prediction error supplies an energy score for each candidate. This score penalizes inconsistent plans and is combined with value estimates to choose actions. It provides a learned feasibility signal alongside the planner’s assessment of expected benefit.

SAGE fits pipelines that sample trajectories and select actions through value scoring. It needs no environment rollouts or policy retraining, although its encoder and predictor are trained from offline data. Across locomotion, navigation, and manipulation benchmarks, the authors report improved performance and robustness, supporting consistency-aware selection as a useful addition to diffusion planning.
icml-2026-improving-diffusion-planners-b.tldr: SAGE improves diffusion planning by combining value estimates with learned transition-consistency scores when selecting candidate actions.

paragraphs: Graph diffusion models commonly sample with evenly spaced time steps, even though the generated distribution can change at very different rates along the trajectory. This paper chooses sampling steps using the geometry of those distributional changes. It views the evolving distribution as a curve on a Riemannian manifold, where distance reflects statistical change.

The Fisher-Rao metric supplies the distance measure. From it, the authors derive a Drift Variation Score that tracks the instantaneous rate of distributional evolution. Their solver uses this signal to maintain constant informational speed, distributing sampling steps by equal geometric arc length. The aim is to make successive steps comparable in how much they change the distribution, rather than simply in elapsed diffusion time.

The theoretical analysis connects the score to local stiffness of the sampling dynamics in the Fisher-Rao sense. Experiments on molecular and social-network generation report significant improvements in structural fidelity and sampling efficiency. These results support adapting computation to the statistical geometry of graph generation instead of relying on a uniform schedule.
icml-2026-information-geometric-adaptive.tldr: A Fisher-Rao-based sampling score adapts graph diffusion steps to distributional change, improving reported graph fidelity and sampling efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement-learning agents that can alter the rules governing their environment’s transitions. In the usual formulation, an agent chooses actions within a given environment to maximize long-term discounted reward. Here, some actions can reconfigure the underlying dynamics themselves, potentially making future interaction more rewarding.

The proposed formalism is a multi-layer configurable time-varying Markov decision process. At the lower level, a conventional action policy operates in an environment whose transition function can change over time. At the upper level, configuration actions determine changes to that transition function. The layers distinguish acting within a configuration from choosing how the environment is configured.

The learning objective therefore combines two policy problems: choosing useful configurations and choosing effective primitive actions under those configurations. Both contribute to expected long-term reward, so they must be considered jointly. The abstract presents this modeling framework and objective rather than an empirical performance result. Its contribution is to make deliberate modification of world dynamics an explicit part of the agent’s decision problem.
icml-2026-learn-to-change-the-world-mult.tldr: The paper formalizes reinforcement learning in which agents jointly learn ordinary actions and higher-level actions that reconfigure environment dynamics.

paragraphs: Mind-Omni brings brain, visual, and language modeling into one framework spanning seven encoding and decoding tasks. The motivation is that separate models for individual tasks restrict versatility and miss opportunities for tasks to benefit one another. A unified system can learn relationships among external stimuli and neural representations within shared machinery.

Its Brain Tokenizer converts heterogeneous continuous brain signals into standardized discrete tokens. These tokens enable interactions with other modalities at the token level in a common semantic space. A discrete diffusion framework supports understanding and generation involving two or more modalities. The authors also construct a Brain Question Answering instruction-tuning dataset to develop more advanced reasoning capabilities.

The paper reports state-of-the-art performance among unified multi-task frameworks and evidence that learning tasks together is beneficial. Performance is competitive with larger specialized models and sometimes exceeds them. Those comparisons support the feasibility of a versatile model for neural activity, while the shared token representation provides the mechanism for connecting brain signals with vision and language.
icml-2026-mind-omni-a-unified-multi-task.tldr: Mind-Omni tokenizes brain signals and uses discrete diffusion to unify seven brain–vision–language tasks with reported benefits from joint learning.

paragraphs: MixReasoning addresses unnecessary elaboration inside long reasoning responses. A problem may contain a few difficult decisions alongside many straightforward calculations or revisions. Giving every step the same detailed treatment can waste output length. The framework changes reasoning depth within a single response so that easy and difficult portions receive different treatment.

The method trains a lightweight LoRA adapter that encourages concise reasoning. During generation, it estimates difficulty from token confidence measured over a sliding window and adjusts the adapter’s strength to switch modes. The resulting response can alternate between detailed reasoning for challenging steps and shorter inference for simpler ones, rather than committing to one style throughout.

Across AIME24, MATH-500, GPQA, and GSM8K, the authors report reasoning-length reductions of 13%–49% while maintaining performance. These are gains in the length of generated reasoning, with reductions varying across benchmarks. The findings support fine-grained control of elaboration as a practical way to improve reasoning efficiency while preserving the tested models’ answer performance.
icml-2026-mixreasoning-switching-modes-t.tldr: MixReasoning switches between concise and detailed reasoning within a response, reducing reported reasoning length by 13%–49% while maintaining performance.

paragraphs: MoST integrates speech and text in a mixture-of-experts language model. Its starting point is that speech and text have different representational patterns, so applying identical parameters to both can overlook useful distinctions. The architecture routes tokens according to modality while retaining shared components that allow information to transfer between speech and language.

Modality-specific expert groups learn patterns particular to each input type, and shared experts support cross-modal understanding. The training pipeline adapts a pretrained mixture-of-experts language model using speech recognition and speech synthesis datasets, then fine-tunes it on speech-text instructions. All datasets used in this pipeline are fully accessible and open source.

Evaluations cover speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio language modeling, and spoken question answering. MoST consistently outperforms existing models with comparable parameter counts, and ablations show that both modality-specific routing and shared experts contribute significantly across tested domains. The findings support combining specialization with sharing, and the authors describe MoST as, to their knowledge, the first fully open-source speech-text LLM based on mixture-of-experts architecture.
icml-2026-most-mixing-speech-and-text-wi.tldr: MoST combines modality-specific and shared experts to improve speech-text tasks using an adaptation pipeline built entirely from open datasets.

paragraphs: ParaX adapts pretrained vision models while training relatively few parameters. The paper targets two weaknesses of existing efficient adaptation methods: their behavior can be insufficiently responsive to the input, and different layers can learn redundant representations. These issues are particularly relevant to complex dense prediction tasks.

The method treats trainable parameter matrices as experts in a shared collection called an expert center. During a forward pass, each adapter module selectively combines matrices from its corresponding center to construct weights suited to that module and the current input. These dynamically generated weights provide input-dependent low-rank adaptation. Multiple layers share an expert center, creating implicit interaction between their representations and encouraging feature diversity.

Experiments across diverse visual recognition tasks report superior performance for ParaX. The distinctive contribution is that routing determines the parameters used for adaptation, enabling customization without separately learning a complete set of weights for every layer and input. The reported findings support dynamic parameter assembly and cross-layer sharing as useful mechanisms for efficient vision-model adaptation.
icml-2026-parameters-as-experts-adapting.tldr: ParaX assembles input-dependent adapter weights from shared parameter experts to improve efficient adaptation of vision models.

paragraphs: PASO targets the sequential dependence of gradient-based training: an optimizer ordinarily needs one update before it can compute the next. The paper reframes the entire update trajectory as a system of triangular nonlinear equations. This opens a route to computing gradients associated with different optimization steps concurrently.

The theoretical framework establishes that the equation system has a unique solution matching the original gradient-descent trajectory. It also gives convergence to that trajectory within no more solver iterations than the corresponding number of sequential steps. PASO builds on this formulation to accelerate a broad class of optimizers, including SGD and Adam, by solving for multiple steps in parallel.

Experiments including Llama-3.2-1B and a diffusion model report up to a 21-fold reduction in gradient-descent steps and a 4.5-fold wall-clock speedup, without model-quality loss. The difference between those figures matters: fewer sequential steps and less elapsed training time are distinct outcomes. The results support exploiting parallelism across optimization steps while preserving the target training trajectory.
icml-2026-paso-step-parallel-stochastic-.tldr: PASO reformulates sequential optimization as an equation-solving problem to parallelize training steps, reporting up to 4.5-fold wall-clock acceleration.

paragraphs: PATRA addresses two obstacles in answering questions about time series. A language model needs to recognize temporal patterns relevant to the question, and it needs sufficient reasoning ability to use them. Treating measurements only as text or images can obscure trends and seasonal behavior, while mixed-difficulty training can allow easier objectives to dominate.

The model introduces a pattern-aware mechanism that extracts trends and seasonality from time series to improve alignment with the language-based task. It also uses a task-aware balanced reward to harmonize learning across difficulty levels. This reward encourages coherent chains of thought while addressing the imbalance that can prevent more demanding reasoning tasks from receiving effective training.

Experiments report that PATRA outperforms strong baselines across diverse time-series question-answering tasks, with better cross-modal understanding and reasoning. The approach matters because it addresses both the representation of temporal evidence and the incentives used to learn from it. Its reported gains support combining explicit temporal-pattern extraction with rewards that account for differences in task difficulty.
icml-2026-patra-pattern-aware-alignment-.tldr: PATRA combines trend and seasonality extraction with difficulty-aware rewards to improve time-series question answering.

paragraphs: PhoStream evaluates whether multimodal assistants can handle continuous audio and video in mobile settings. Understanding a completed recording does not capture the full challenge of following a live stream: an assistant must also determine when enough evidence has arrived to respond. The benchmark includes both activity on the phone screen and events outside it.

The dataset contains 5,572 open-ended question-answer pairs drawn from 578 videos, covering four scenarios and ten capabilities. An automated generation pipeline is combined with human verification. Models are tested through an online inference pipeline, and an LLM judge evaluates their open-ended answers. This setup makes response timing part of the evaluation setting.

Results show a strong temporal imbalance. Gemini 3 Pro scores above 80 on Instant and Backward tasks on the judge’s 0–100 scale, but scores 16.40 on Forward tasks. The authors largely attribute this decline to answering before necessary visual and audio cues appear. The benchmark therefore exposes response timing as a substantial weakness in the evaluated streaming assistants.
icml-2026-phostream-benchmarking-real-wo.tldr: PhoStream tests mobile assistants on live audiovisual streams and reveals that premature responses sharply undermine tasks requiring future evidence.

paragraphs: NaviEdit addresses the tension between making a substantial semantic edit and preserving an image’s structure. The authors identify a primary cause in existing diffusion and flow editing: stronger edits are coupled to traversal through noisier model states. Those states can disrupt layout before the intended change has been localized.

The proposed controller operates during inference and leaves the pretrained model unchanged. It separates edit progress from scale traversal through a strict self-consistency condition. Scale becomes a control input, allowing a fixed number of computation steps to be redistributed toward intermediate scales that respond to semantic changes. This reduces reliance on high-noise regimes that can damage structure.

Experiments show positive average gains across compatible editors and flow backbones. The qualification matters: the abstract reports average improvements within compatible systems, rather than improvement for every edit or model. The findings support a portable inference-time control principle in which the allocation of editing steps can be changed without training the underlying generator again.
icml-2026-semantic-granularity-navigatio.tldr: NaviEdit reallocates a fixed editing budget across model scales, improving average results in compatible systems without retraining.

paragraphs: SGB-IB groups samples using information from multiple modalities while adapting the level of detail at which relationships are represented. A single granularity creates a trade-off: fine detail can be affected by local variation and redundant disturbances, while coarse groups can erase useful neighborhood structure. The method introduces adaptive groups to address both problems.

These groups are granular-balls, hyperspheres containing similar samples. The algorithm begins with the whole dataset in one ball and recursively splits it using a purity measure. That measure averages the mutual information between sample features and K-means-derived pseudo-labels across modalities. A structure-aware objective then balances preservation of local relationships against suppression of global redundancy.

The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets. Their findings support combining adaptive grouping with information-theoretic objectives for multimodal clustering. The mechanism matters because it allows the representation’s granularity to vary with the data while explicitly balancing the local structure needed for grouping against information that adds redundancy.
icml-2026-structure-aware-granular-ball-.tldr: SGB-IB uses adaptively split groups and an information-based objective to preserve local structure while reducing redundancy in multimodal clustering.

paragraphs: SurrogateSHAP estimates how much different data contributors matter to a text-to-image model’s outputs. Shapley values provide a principled attribution framework, but computing them is costly when it requires retraining models on many contributor subsets. Interactions among contributors also make the number of combinations difficult to manage.

The method approximates the retraining-based attribution problem using inference from a pretrained model. It then fits a gradient-boosted tree to approximate the utility function and derives Shapley values analytically from that tree. This avoids repeated retraining of the image generator while making the attribution calculation more tractable. The resulting values describe contributions to the chosen utility measure.

Evaluations cover image quality, artistic aesthetics, and product diversity across three generation settings. The authors report better performance than prior attribution methods, substantially lower computational overhead, and consistent identification of influential contributors. They also demonstrate localization of data sources behind spurious correlations in clinical images. This connects contributor valuation with auditing which data sources influence undesirable generation behavior.
icml-2026-surrogateshap-training-free-co.tldr: SurrogateSHAP approximates contributor Shapley values without retraining image generators, supporting efficient valuation and data-source auditing.

paragraphs: This paper studies how language models maintain their usual helpful Assistant persona despite being able to represent many identities. Across several models, the authors identify an activation-space direction that tracks how strongly the model is operating in its default Assistant mode. They call this direction the Assistant Axis.

Steering activations toward that direction reinforces helpful and harmless behavior, while steering away increases identification with other entities. Deviations along the axis also predict persona drift, in which behavior becomes harmful or bizarre relative to the model’s usual persona. In the studied conversations, drift is often driven by requests for reflection on the model’s processes or interactions featuring emotionally vulnerable users.

Restricting activations to a fixed region along the axis stabilizes behavior in these scenarios and against adversarial persona-based jailbreaks. The findings suggest that post-training places models near an Assistant-like region without firmly anchoring them there. They support monitoring and controlling internal representations as a way to improve persona stability in the examined settings.
icml-2026-the-assistant-axis-situating-a.tldr: An internal Assistant Axis predicts persona drift across several models, and constraining activations along it stabilizes behavior in tested scenarios.

paragraphs: TraCeS learns safety-related feedback when supervision says only whether an entire trajectory was acceptable. Such approvals and rejections do not directly identify which moments contributed to a violation. This makes policy learning difficult when neither an explicit safety cost nor the threshold defining an unacceptable trajectory is known.

The method trains a sequential estimator that assigns violation credit at each time step. Those credits factorize its predicted probability that the trajectory has avoided violation up to that point. This links local learning signals to the available whole-trajectory labels. The estimated signal is then incorporated into constrained policy optimization and remains compatible with standard continuous-control algorithms.

The paper analyzes the approximation gap introduced by its learning objective. Experiments report improved constraint satisfaction and more efficient use of feedback relative to baselines across continuous-control benchmarks, including long tasks and noisy or inconsistent labels. The contribution is a structured way to extract per-step training guidance from sparse overall judgments, without requiring a known cost function or violation threshold.
icml-2026-traces-learning-per-timestep-c.tldr: TraCeS converts whole-trajectory safety judgments into per-step violation signals for constrained reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies online optimization with diminishing returns, where increasing a decision variable can have smaller benefits as other variables grow. The functions are non-monotone, so increasing a variable can also reduce the objective. Decisions lie in down-closed convex sets, which allow feasible coordinates to be reduced while remaining feasible.

The central result establishes a structural property called 1/e-upper-linearizability for this function class. It requires a carefully chosen exponential reparametrization, scaling parameter, and surrogate potential. Together, these constructions enable a reduction to online linear optimization. This provides a route to stronger guarantees for the original nonlinear problem through a more tractable optimization framework.

The resulting method achieves optimal square-root-in-T static regret with one gradient query per round. The framework also provides adaptive and dynamic regret guarantees and improved rates under semi-bandit, bandit, and zeroth-order feedback. The authors state that their bounds strictly improve prior results across the feedback models studied. These are theoretical guarantees for the specified function class and feasible-set structure.
icml-2026-upper-linearizability-of-onlin.tldr: A new upper-linearizability result reduces a class of online diminishing-returns problems to linear optimization and strengthens regret guarantees.

paragraphs: VisualScore evaluates multiple dimensions of image quality within one model. Technical quality, aesthetics, and agreement with a text prompt involve different criteria, and their reward scales can conflict during reinforcement learning. The framework combines task-aware reasoning with numerical scoring so that an assessment includes both a rationale and a scalar score.

The authors construct a reasoning-enhanced reward-modeling dataset through rejection sampling and use it for supervised initialization. They then train with Group Relative Policy Optimization and a Gaussian-based continuous reward. Standard deviation filtering and entropy gating normalize reward signals across tasks and suppress noisy updates, addressing instability caused by different reward scales and variances.

Experiments across technical quality, aesthetics, and text–image alignment report improved robustness, generalization, and interpretability. VisualScore can also guide text-to-image generation at test time without retraining. The contribution connects explicit evaluation principles with training controls for multiple scoring tasks, supporting a single evaluator that can explain its judgments and use them to influence generated images.
icml-2026-visualscore-learning-holistic-.tldr: VisualScore learns explanations and numerical image-quality scores across tasks while controlling reward conflicts during reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: WarmServe addresses a trade-off in serving several language models on shared GPUs: higher utilization can come with slower responses, especially before the first token appears. The authors connect this delay to systems that do not anticipate future demand. Their approach uses forecasts motivated by the periodicity and long-term predictability observed in real serving workloads.

The system proactively loads weights from multiple models onto GPUs so that serving instances can start promptly when requests surge. Its placement algorithm limits interference among prewarming decisions. A cache-reservation strategy uses idle key-value cache space on running GPUs to hold additional model weights, and a memory-switching mechanism manages the tensors efficiently.

On real-world datasets, WarmServe reduces tail time-to-first-token by up to 50.8-fold relative to a state-of-the-art autoscaling system. It also supports up to 2.5 times the request throughput of a GPU-sharing system. These comparisons concern different baselines and outcomes. Together, they show how forecast-driven weight preparation can improve response latency and serving capacity in the evaluated workloads.
icml-2026-warmserve-enabling-one-for-man.tldr: WarmServe forecasts demand and preloads multiple models’ weights onto shared GPUs to improve response latency and throughput.
